actual_new_QFT_source_change_u3.genuine_before_excerpt: 2.1 To apply [F2] with one-particle space $\mathcal H_T$, first verify its separability hypothesis. Let $D$ be the countable dense subset of real $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ supplied by [F4]. Its sixfold product is countable by [F5]; identifying each tuple with a three-component complex function whose real and imaginary components lie in $D$ gives a dense subset of $\mathcal H$. Density follows by approximating the six real $L^2$ components, since the squared complex-vector norm is the sum of their squared norms. Hence $\mathcal H$ is separable in its norm topology by [F6]. The image of this countable set under the bounded projection $M_{P_T}$ is countable and dense in $\mathcal H_T$: for $u\in\mathcal H_T$, $M_{P_T}u=u$, so projected approximants to $u$ converge to $u$. Thus $\mathcal H_T$ is separable in its norm topology by [F6], and [F2] applies. By [F3], a vector in $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ has only finitely many nonzero sectors. On each such sector [F2] bounds creation and annihilation by the corresponding square-root particle number times $\|g_j\|\|\Psi_n\|$. Thus both maps and their sum are defined on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. The same estimates bound every matrix element between fixed finite-particle vectors by a constant times $\|g_j\|$. On each fixed compact support, repeated integration by parts in step 1.1 bounds $\|g_j\|$ by finitely many smooth-test seminorms, so these matrix elements are continuous in the test-function topology. This proves the asserted distributional smearing without defining a point field. [F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, given]
